text:
I found no direct study comparing recent-suffix cropping against exactly matched target-position loss weighting in NextItNet. The closest is [Zhou et al., WWW 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.11136v1): they disable RecBole’s default sliding-window augmentation, distinguish last-target supervision from supervision across historical targets, and compare eight augmentation operators. They control crop length and augmentation multiplicity, but do not jointly match target identities, target frequencies, removed context, and optimization budget. Importantly, adding cropping to sliding-window training generally underperforms sliding windows alone. This supports treating additional supervision as a possible confound, rather than assuming cropping itself helps.

[CL4SRec](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.14395) uses cropped views for an auxiliary contrastive objective alongside recommendation training; it does not isolate suffix context removal against matched recency-weighted supervision. [NextItNet](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.05163) already trains autoregressively across sequence positions using causal dilated convolutions. Architectural inference: for stride-one convolutions, receptive-field width is R = 1 + Σ(kℓ−1)dℓ, counting every convolution. With position-local normalization and no global sequence features, removing context outside a retained output’s receptive field cannot change that output; cropping inside it can. Training dropout can still change individual stochastic realizations.

The decisive experiment is therefore a paired ablation within one NextItNet: sample identical target positions and negatives; compare cropped contexts with full contexts using identical target masks, weights, loss normalization, and update counts. Include full-context recency weighting alone. Measure retained targets and removed context within R, then evaluate each trained model separately with both cropped and full histories to quantify inference mismatch. These are proposed controls, not controls established by the cited studies.
